https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-thousand.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iw7U Indonesian authorities have set up field hospitals to treat the wounded and house displaced people Image: Edgar Su/REUTERS Advertisement The death toll from the 7.7-magnitude earthquake which hit eastern Indonesia this weekend rose to at least 68 on Monday, casting a shadow over the country's Independence Day celebrations. Over 100 more people have been injured but local authorities do not believe anybody is missing. The quake's epicenter was located off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles) on Saturday, the US Geological Survey (USGS) said. It has since been followed by almost 1,600 smaller aftershocks, including a 5.6-magnitude jolt on Monday morning. A tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks, was later lifted. But around 500 houses have been damaged and roads have been blocked by landslides, leaving around 12,800 people on Flores unable to return to their homes. Some earthquake victims have criticized the authorities' response to the disaster Image: Juni Kriswanto/AFP Indonesia residents: 'We need aid as soon as possible' "Our houses are no longer inhabitable, because many have collapsed and are full of cracks, so we can't go inside anymore," one resident told the AFP news agency outside a self-made tent that was sleeping about 30 people. "We only go back home to get water, clothes, pillows, and then we spend the nights here." Other residents complained to the Reuters news agency about poor conditions in such tents, with some children contracting diarrhea and at least one older person suffering a stroke. "I can only eat rice with nothing else," said one young mother whose baby was wrapped in a brown blanket in the back of a pickup truck. "We need aid as soon as possible. ⁠We are ​just salt farmers." Why does Indonesia keep getting hit by major earthquakes? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Indonesia: how is the government responding? On Sunday evening, Indonesia's disaster mitigation agency, known as BNPB, said the Indonesian Air Force was preparing to bring 13 tons of emergency aid to the region. The country's deputy health minister, Benjamin Paulus ⁠Octavianus, said the military was also planning to construct an emergency field hospital but said neurosurgeons and orthopedic surgeons were needed to treat head injuries and broken bones. The earthquake is Indonesia's deadliest disaster since a 2022 quake killed hundreds in West Java, and has overshadowed the country's Independence Day celebrations marking independence from Japanese rule in 1945. President Prabowo Subianto marked the occasion by presiding over celebrations in the capital, Jakarta, about 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) west of the ​disaster zone. But the festivities were the last thing on the mind of residents affected by the earthquake, with one father telling Reuters: "I'm not thinking about that anymore. I'm just thinking about the safety of my wife and 4-year-old twins." Indonesia's history of earthquakes Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan. Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region: 1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people 2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra, triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean 2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa 2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing Edited by: Natalie Muller Advertisement Skip next section More on Catastrophe from Asia More on Catastrophe from Asia India temple stampede in Bihar kills 7 At least seven people were killed after a stampede broke out at a Hindu shrine in eastern India. https://www.politico.eu/article/block-us.text: EU lawmakers are calling for the Commission to forbid European firms and banks from applying U.S. sanctions, as Washington weighs sanctioning the International Criminal Court over its actions concerning Israel. The U.S. has already targeted nine of the court’s judges and four prosecutors since the Netherlands-based institution issued a warrant for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. “To protect its values, [the EU] needs to protect the ICC and the people who work there. It means … activating the blocking statute,” said Dutch lawmaker Dirk Gotink of the center-right European People’s Party after a closed-door meeting of the economy committee on Monday evening. Advertisement Advertisement U.S. sanctions on the ICC, which is based in The Hague, would present it with numerous operational challenges such as paying staff, accessing IT services and maintaining its detention facilities. The blocking statute could protect the court by preventing European companies from complying with U.S. sanctions. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul on Monday visited the ICC in a show of support. His appearance was notable given Germany’s otherwise stalwart backing for Israel. At a joint press conference with Wadephul, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen called the blocking statute the “nuclear option,” the AP reported. The Dutch government has been in touch with the Commission to ensure it can be quickly enacted, the Foreign Affairs Ministry told POLITICO. French judge Nicolas Guillou, speaking at the economy committee hearing, said: “What’s at stake is whether we are going to be a democracy in the 21st century,” adding: “Will there be the rule of law in Europe?” “We are in between terrorists from al Qaeda and Daesh, with some kleptocrats and some international drug traffickers in the same list.” Guillou is one 13 ICC officials that the U.S. has sanctioned , including its president, Tomoko Akane of Japan. Advertisement Advertisement French Socialist and economy committee chair Aurore Lalucq said: “What’s happening ... is a major test for Europe. It is also a test of our political will. Do we want to give up on our values or not?” She called for the Commission to intervene at the highest political level. “We know that the U.S. administration only functions with signals of clarity,” Gotink agreed. “What we need is leadership from the Commission.” The Dutch politician insisted that one big problem is the overcompliance of European financial firms with Washington sanctions. “Banks in Europe automatically apply American sanctions, no questions asked. Within one hour, a couple of hours, you are blocked from your account,” he said. “This automaticity stems from the time when we thought that the Americans were still our friends. Of course we take over sanctions from the Americans. They liberated our continent. But that time is over, and we need to stop automatically following the State Department, knowing also what kind of policies are currently being developed in that place.” Their voices add to a growing chorus of European politicians standing up for the court, which has 125 member countries around the world.

Photograph: Chedly Ben Ibrahim/NurPhoto via Getty Images FBI US seized American heir’s cellphone in violation of treaty agreement, lawyer says James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, in prison in Spain, has applied for asylum as US seeks extradition over alleged Hamas support Timothy Pratt Sun 25 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 05.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US authorities seized wealthy activist James “Fergie” Chambers’s cellphone at some point after Spanish police arrested him in July without notifying him or his attorneys, the Guardian has learned. Chambers, a US citizen and wealthy donor to leftwing and humanitarian projects, is imprisoned in Madrid. His case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation tied to money Chambers has donated to support Palestinians, including the Sameer Project , in Gaza. The extradition request also includes charges associated with a protest against Elbit Systems, an Israeli weapons manufacturer. Chambers’s legal team discovered that the phone was no longer in the custody of the national court in Madrid and had been turned over to the FBI upon inquiring about it Tuesday, according to attorney Aitor Martínez. This occurred despite the team having received written guarantees from the court that the phone “would remain under the court’s custody while the extradition request was resolved” – as both Spanish law and the extradition treaty between the two countries require, Martínez said. “I’ve never seen anything like this in an extradition case,” he said. “Spanish judicial authorities can’t surrender control over the personal effects of a person sought in extradition just because a foreign government has asked for them … and now a judge has secretly turned over Fergie’s phone to the US.” The defense has filed a petition with an appeals court seeking immediate return of the phone – as well as a detailed explanation of the phone’s chain of custody, who authorized what and when and whether or not the US had accessed the phone’s contents. It is assumed the office of Félix Bolaños, the Spanish minister of justice, would have to get involved in bringing the phone back, Martínez said. Chambers has asserted through his attorneys and partner, the actor and activist Stella Schnabel, that the extradition is politically motivated. He has applied for political asylum from prison. Under Spanish law, an asylum applicant cannot be extradited until the asylum process is completed. He remains imprisoned after a judge denied a petition for provisional release earlier this month, asserting in part that his wealth made him a flight risk. Chambers, a self-described communist and anti-imperialist, is heir of the Cox family, owners of Atlanta-based Cox Communications. As part of a settlement in which his family severed ties with him at the time, he sold stock back to his family worth about $250m in mid-2023. Since then, he has been funding an estimated 100 projects in 20 countries, according to Schnabel. Chambers’s views and donations have been extensively profiled in US media, and his public comments on Israel and Gaza have brought controversy. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.” His legal team is now asserting that various Spanish and international laws governing both extradition and political asylum have been violated by US authorities seizing his the phone without legal due process. The Spanish courts are handling the extradition case and could take months to decide whether to hand Chambers over to the US. Meanwhile, Martínez noted, a 1970 treaty between the two countries stipulates that the possessions of a person sought in extradition can only be released to the requesting country – in this case, the United States – if and when extradition has been granted. As for the political asylum claim, “Chambers’s status as an asylum applicant means the court can’t ignore its obligations to protect him, or give information about him to the country alleged to be persecuting him,” Martínez said. Schnabel told the Guardian she retrieved Chambers’s personal effects last month at the prison where he is detained, including keys and identification. It is unclear whether Spain had already surrendered his phone to the US by then; Martínez said that the judge assured him on 20 July that the phone was in the court’s custody. “I’m not surprised,” said Schnabel, referring to the apparent suspension of due process driven by the FBI’s request. “It’s exactly in line with this administration not following the rules of the legal system.” Explore more on these topics FBI Trump administration Spain US justice system US crime US foreign policy Europe Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.portfolio.hu/global/20261113.text: A cseh Aero Vodochody vállalat által gyártott L-39 Skyfox egy szubszonikus sugárhajtású kiképzőgép, amelyet elsősorban katonai pilóták felkészítésére terveztek. Emellett azonban könnyű támadó, felderítő és légi járőrözési feladatok ellátására is alkalmas, így hatékonyan bevethető a drónok elleni védekezésben. Petr Macinka a cseh televíziónak adott interjújában elmondta, hogy az első négy repülőgép pénzügyi háttere már biztosított, és személyesen tárgyaltak a gyártóval annak érdekében, hogy az ukrán megrendelést soron kívül, kiemelt prioritással teljesítsék. Az átadáshoz ugyanakkor még szükség van bizonyos külföldi – többek között amerikai, francia és belga – alkatrészek és avionikai rendszerek exportengedélyeire. A teljes flotta kiépítéséhez Csehország és Ukrajna még júliusban tizenkét országot – köztük Ausztráliát, Kanadát és tíz európai államot – keresett meg, hogy segítsenek további tizenkét gép megvásárlásában. A teljes üzlet értéke eléri a 6–8 milliárd cseh koronát (272–363 millió dollárt), amelyet teljes egészében nemzetközi forrásokból fedeznek, így Prága a saját központi költségvetéséből nem különít el erre pénzt. A tizenhat gépes beszerzés részleteiről Karel Havlíček cseh ipari és kereskedelmi miniszter is tárgyalt Kijevben Szerhij Koreckij ukrán miniszterelnökkel. A megbeszélésen megerősítették, hogy négy repülőgépről már megszületett a végleges megállapodás, a fennmaradó tizenkettőről pedig előzetes egyezség van érvényben. A mostani üzlet előzménye, hogy korábban L-159-es könnyű harci gépek átadása is felmerült az orosz drónok elleni védekezés céljából. Prága azonban januárban elutasította, hogy a saját haderejének állományából adjon el vagy adjon át ilyen repülőgépeket, mivel azokra a cseh fegyveres erőknek is szükségük van.
